name: Luhman 16
kind: The closest pair of brown dwarfs, 6.5 light-years away (not in Gaia's main catalogue)

reference.source: Gaia DR3 5353626573555863424 position (2016.0); motion and parallax from Bedin et al. 2017, MNRAS 470, 1140

gaia_facts.note: Not in Gaia DR3; parallax from Gaia DR3 5353626573555863424 position (2016.0); motion and parallax from Bedin et al. 2017, MNRAS 470, 1140

evidence.classification: Nearby object with fast proper motion (published motion)

checks.text: Measured speed matches the catalogue: 2.83 vs 2.78″/yr (difference 1.6%)

No Gaia DR3 counterpart: too faint or too cold for Gaia's visible-light camera. Catalogued in the literature (Gaia DR3 5353626573555863424 position (2016.0); motion and parallax from Bedin et al. 2017, MNRAS 470, 1140).

numbers.label: catalogue motion (Gaia DR3 5353626573555863424 position (2016.0); motion and parallax from Bedin et al. 2017)

items.reason: This is the mission target itself: both ends lie on its measured path.

changes.method: Dots seen only in WISE 2010 are paired with dots seen only in SPHEREx at 4.6 µm, 8″ to 190″ apart and of similar brightness. Each pair is then checked against the target's path, Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD.
changes.not_checked: Asteroids and comets are not checked. An unconfirmed pair is not a discovery.

facts.headline: About 27 km/s across the sky
facts.detail: That is 0.9 times the speed of Earth around the Sun. It is sideways speed only: motion toward or away from us does not show in images.

facts.headline: Crosses the width of the full Moon in about 640 years
facts.detail: A typical star in these images needs more than 100,000 years, which is why this one stands out in a flipbook.

facts.headline: 6.5 light-years away: one of the Sun's nearest neighbours
facts.detail: The light in these images left it about 6.5 years ago.
facts.basis: 3.26 ÷ parallax (″), Gaia DR3 5353626573555863424 position (2016.0); motion and parallax from Bedin et al. 2017, MNRAS 470, 1140

facts.headline: Invisible to Gaia's visible-light camera
facts.detail: It shows up only in infrared light. Objects like this are what an infrared survey can find and a visible-light survey cannot.
facts.basis: no Gaia DR3 source at the predicted position

limits: Motion: an object must shift 2 SPHEREx pixels (12″) to count as moving. Over these 16.0 years that means faster than 0.77″ per year. Slower objects read as “no measurable motion”.
SPHEREx alone covers only 12 months here: by the same 2-pixel rule, enough only for motion faster than 13″ per year. The 2010 WISE image is what makes slower motion visible.
Brightness: compared at 3 SPHEREx visits only. A change between or outside those dates is not seen.
Solar System: the page checks against Gaia stars only. It does not check asteroids or comets, so a moving dot without a Gaia circle may be a known asteroid.
Crowding: one SPHEREx pixel is 6.15″ wide, so two close objects can blend into one dot and one spectrum.
